description: ​We are a passionate team of STEM school students dedicated to solving real-world challenges through technology, science, and creative problem-solving. With strong backgrounds in science, engineering, and mathematics, we are eager to collaborate and build an innovative project for this hackathon.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective 3D is an interactive 3D globe, which makes NASA data easy to understand. Users can choose any region on Earth and travel from 2000 to 2024 to know how temperature, humidity, and wind changes. The website uses NASA MERRA-2 data with expectations that follows SSP2-4.5.
What is changing is shown by comparing each region’s long-term average forecast. where it is changing is shown by letting the users explore any location on the globe, since the trends could be different between regions. How much it is changing through the years from 2000 to 2040. The Mann-Kendall test shows if the change is significant, showing the real trends from the inaccurate random ones.

The website contains Simple, Normal, and Complex, supports two languages, which are Arabic and English, includes farm and polar labs, and shows how changes affect the crops, snow, and even people.
NASA data is large but the challenging part is finding what the user needs from it. We gathered 40 years of data and projections in one website, warn users about high heat and wind, as it helps farmers test the variables affecting the crops through simulation.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Earth Detective is an interactive Web-site that turns NASA Earth data into a story anyone can follow. The user spins a 3D globe, taps a country, and chooses one variable: temperature, humidity, or wind speed. A Time Machine timeline lets them pick any month from 2000 to 2040. Past dates show observed or reanalysis data. Future dates show a statistical projection, always with an uncertainty band.

The Web-site follows the four steps of the challenge. It takes monthly NASA MERRA-2 data and averages it over the chosen country. It optionally removes the seasonal cycle, then measures the trend as a slope per decade. It tests the trend with the Mann-Kendall test, a t-test, and 95% confidence intervals, and gives a plain verdict: “This trend is real” or “Not significant yet. A longer record might change this.”

For each country and date, the user also gets:

  • the causes of the change
  • impacts on a branch they choose (health, economy, farming, water, energy, and more)
  • climate alerts
  • past disasters and predicted risk
  • real sourced human reports
  • a daily tip specific to that country

When the user switches to complicated mode, it previews effects on: surface skin temperature, snow cover and sea ice, ozone column in the temperature branch. In the humidity branch, precipitation flux, evaporation/evapotranspiration, soil moisture & stream flow are shown. In the wind speed branch, vegetation greenness, aerosol optical depth, nitrogen dioxide air pollution. All of these effects are shown for every place on the globe.

 GLDAS, GPM, MODIS, AIRS, and OMI provide context for the causes.

What benefits does it have?

  • Anyone can use real science. Simple, Normal, and Complicated modes change the language, visuals, and depth of every button and chart, from a student (B1 English, many visuals) to a researcher (p-values, confidence intervals, citations).
  • It teaches how to think about data. Users learn to ask whether a trend is real or just luck.
  • It is honest. Every number is labeled observed, reanalysis, or projected, and forecasts never appear without uncertainty.
  • Support is built in. There is a manual voice narrator, a glossary, a notebook, a Gemini co-pilot, and an in-app guide.

What is the intended impact?

We want to lower the barrier to NASA climate data, so that all different types of people can get a tested conclusion about any country they choose on the Earth globe. Showing the impacts on global economics, health and other stuff helps to connect the data to real-life awareness of climate risks and helps to understand how the situation is going.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software were used?

Data and science: NASA MERRA-2 (or the NASA POWER API), GLDAS, GPM, MODIS, AIRS, OMI, NASA EONET, ReliefWeb, NOAA, and Natural Earth boundaries.

Planned technical stack: TypeScript with Next.js and React, Three.js (react-three-fiber) for the globe, D3 or ECharts for charts, Python (FastAPI) for the statistics, PostgreSQL and Redis for storage and caching, Firebase or Supabase for sign-in, and the Gemini API through a secure backend for the co-pilot and daily tips.

Hardware: standard laptops, with no special hardware needed.

How is it creative?

·        Catchy tip. A relatively small alien flies around the globe. When the user clicks on it it presents a tip for : Web-site tips, health and safety, Earth care and  jokes.

  • A time machine. One timeline moves the whole Web-site through the past, the present, and the future.
  • Visual Farm and Polar Place. Users set temperature, humidity, and wind, and watch crops or ice respond, following documented rules and not random animation.
  • The same science, three ways. Every content block is written in three real versions, not just restyled.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Audience: students and the public, with researchers in mind too, which led to the three levels and simple definitions. Blind users are able to use manual only-voice narrator.
  • Scientific honesty: reanalysis is not raw measurement, monthly data is autocorrelated, and a country average can hide regional differences. Disaster predictions are probabilistic and not official warnings, and the AI must cite data, say “I don’t know,” and never invent numbers.
  • Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA, color-blind-safe palettes, a manual-only voice narrator, reduced-motion support. We made sure to include two widely used languages which are Arabic and English for users.
  • Reliability: cached data and a bundled fallback dataset, so the app still works if a NASA service is slow.
  • Privacy and security: sign-in is required, the Gemini key stays on the server, and users can delete their data.
  • Design: Many visuals are added to keep the user’s attention. Visuals are styled as games. The design is made in an Intermediate and simple way to make all the users find their experience easier.
